Create spatial cross-validation folds

Source: R/cross-validation.R
make_folds.Rd

Builds train and test splits of a layer for cross-validation, by one of six methods: random k-fold, spatial block k-fold, buffered leave-one-out, leave-location-out, nearest-neighbour distance matching (NNDM) leave-one-out, or its k-fold version (kNNDM). It returns the splits (folds), one row per observation naming the fold that holds it out (assignment), and the settings and diagnostics of the build (params). Pass the result as folds to cv_spatial() or another cv_*() function, map it with plot_folds(), and measure how far the held-out points sit from their training data with fold_separation().

Usage

make_folds(
  points_sf,
  k,
  method = c("random_kfold", "block_kfold", "buffered_loo", "leave_location_out", "nndm",
    "knndm"),
  seed = NULL,
  block_nx = NULL,
  block_ny = NULL,
  block_multiplier = 3,
  block_size = NULL,
  auto_range = FALSE,
  range_frac = 1,
  response_var = NULL,
  group_var = NULL,
  prediction_points = NULL,
  predictor_vars = NULL,
  boundary = NULL,
  buffer = NULL,
  min_train = 0.5,
  phi = NULL,
  drop_empty_blocks = TRUE,
  blocks = NULL,
  balance_tol = 3,
  max_test = NULL
)

Arguments

points_sf

An sf layer of the observations. Z and M are dropped before folding, since distances are measured in x and y. A layer without a CRS is aligned to a boundary, blocks or prediction_points that has one, by the rule in spatialkit-geometry. Rows without a location are dropped (see Value).

k

The number of folds, a single whole number of at least 1; required except for "buffered_loo" and "nndm", which build one fold per held-out point (k = n, or max_test of them when it is given) whatever k is. A fraction, NA or a vector is an error. "block_kfold" lowers k when fewer than k blocks hold points, "leave_location_out" when there are fewer than k groups, and "random_kfold" and "knndm" when the layer has fewer than k rows; those four raise k = 1 to 2, since one fold has no training set. Read the k element of the result rather than assume the value asked for, which params$k_requested keeps. Fewer folds than asked raise a warning of class "spatialkit_k_reduced", whose message gives both counts, the reason and, where there is one, a setting that works; the condition carries them as k_requested and k, so tryCatch(spatialkit_k_reduced = ) or withCallingHandlers() can act on it without reading the text.

method

One of the six methods in the section "Fold methods": "random_kfold" (default), "block_kfold", "buffered_loo", "leave_location_out", "nndm" or "knndm".

seed

Optional integer RNG seed; NULL (default) leaves the draws to the session's RNG state. It draws the partition of "random_kfold", the assignment of groups to folds of "leave_location_out", the packing ties of "block_kfold" and "knndm", the random candidate of "knndm" and, above 4,000 points, its k-means starts, and the max_test subset of "buffered_loo" and "nndm", which are otherwise deterministic. With auto_range = TRUE it is also the seed of estimate_sac_range(), which keeps its own default of 123 when seed is NULL.

block_nx, block_ny

Optional grid dimensions for "block_kfold", each a single whole number of at least 1. Give both, or give one and the other is derived from the extent's aspect ratio so that the blocks are about square. Ignored when block_size or auto_range set the grid.

block_multiplier

A single positive number, default 3. When neither block_size nor block_nx/block_ny is given, the grid aims for block_multiplier * k blocks over the extent, keeping its aspect, so each fold holds out about block_multiplier blocks; an extent more than about block_multiplier * k times as wide as it is tall (or as tall as it is wide) gets a single row (or column) of that many blocks. With 1, every fold is one contiguous area and the score depends on which area each fold gets; with many, the blocks shrink towards single points and the folds approach random k-fold. 3 is a compromise between the two, not a published constant.

block_size

Optional positive number, the minimum block edge length, in the units of the CRS the folds are built in (params$crs): your own CRS's units for projected input, and for lon/lat input those of the metre CRS ensure_projected() chooses, which varies with the data (project the data yourself to fix the units in advance). It takes precedence over block_nx/block_ny and block_multiplier. The blocks built are at least this long on an axis that can hold one, and up to just under twice as long; params$block_width and params$block_height record them. See the section "Block size and the autocorrelation range" for how the grid is laid and for a size that leaves too few blocks.

auto_range

Logical, default FALSE. TRUE estimates the autocorrelation range with estimate_sac_range() and uses it as the minimum block_size; it needs response_var, and an explicit block_size takes precedence. With supplied blocks the range is only compared with them. See the section "Block size and the autocorrelation range".

range_frac

Passed to estimate_sac_range() when auto_range = TRUE: a fitted range beyond the longest lag the empirical variogram was fitted over is refused as unidentified, and the grid falls back to geometry, with a warning. A range within that bound can still be too wide for two blocks. Default 1.

response_var

Name of the response column. Required when auto_range = TRUE. For "block_kfold" a name that is not a column of points_sf is an error whether or not auto_range is set, since the response also feeds the warning on blocks smaller than the range, which a misspelt name would switch off.

group_var

Name of a column of points_sf that identifies the location each observation belongs to. Required for method = "leave_location_out", which keeps every observation from a location in one fold. Repeated measurements at a site split across folds score the model partly on sites it has already seen.

prediction_points

Optional sf layer of the locations the model will predict at, such as the grid from predict_surface(); required for "nndm" and "knndm". A layer of cells or polygons is reduced to representative points first, so the target distances are point to point: a point-to-polygon distance is zero for every cell that holds a training point, which would pull the target towards zero and the folds towards plain leave-one-out. A layer that mixes dimensions or carries M is read in x and y, before and after it is reduced to points (spatialkit-geometry). A prediction point without a location, as given or once brought into the CRS of the folds, takes no part in the target and is not counted in params$n_prediction_points.

predictor_vars

Optional character vector of predictor column names, passed to estimate_sac_range() so that the range is that of the residuals on them.

boundary

Optional polygon layer (sf or sfc) that the block grid of "block_kfold" is clipped to. A cell the boundary only touches at a corner or along an edge is not a block, and a point on the boundary, to the margin in the section "Numerical tolerances", is inside it. See spatialkit-geometry for how a boundary without a CRS is read, and for the rows of a boundary that are left out or refused.

buffer

For "buffered_loo": a single positive number, the distance within which the held-out point's neighbours are excluded from its training set. Like block_size it is in the units of the CRS the folds are built in (params$crs), which for lon/lat input is the metre CRS ensure_projected() chooses: 0.1 means 0.1 m, not 0.1 degrees. A neighbour at the buffer distance is excluded. A buffer that excludes no neighbour from any fold makes the scheme plain leave-one-out, with a warning.

min_train

For "nndm": the smallest fraction of the data any fold's training set may be reduced to by neighbour exclusion; default 0.5, as in CAST::nndm(). Where it binds, the distance matching stops short and the held-out points stay closer to their training data than the prediction points are (see the section "NNDM"). For "knndm": the smallest fraction of the data a fold may leave for training, so a candidate whose largest fold holds more than 1 - min_train of the rows is set aside (the maxp = 0.5 of CAST::knndm() is min_train = 0.5). Equal folds leave 1 - 1/k of the data, so a value above that is an error.

phi

For "nndm": the distance up to which the two nearest-neighbour distance distributions are matched, in the CRS the folds are built in. Matching is attempted only while a held-out point's nearest-neighbour distance is at most phi; the exclusion that takes it past phi is the last one, so a realised distance can exceed phi by up to one neighbour step, as in CAST::nndm(). In Milà et al. (2022) and in CAST::nndm(), \(\phi\) is the autocorrelation range of the outcome: beyond it observations are close to independent, so matching adds nothing. estimate_sac_range() gives such a value. Default NULL: the largest prediction-to-training distance, which matches everywhere (phi = "max" in CAST).

drop_empty_blocks

Logical, default TRUE. With FALSE the blocks that hold no point are kept and packed into folds too, but k is still lowered to the number of blocks that hold points, so no fold is left without test points.

blocks

Optional polygon layer (sf or sfc, POLYGON or MULTIPOLYGON, at least two features) to use as the blocks of "block_kfold" in place of the grid: the $cells of a build_tessellation() result, hexagons, watersheds, administrative units, or the $blocks of blockCV::cv_spatial(). Each point takes the block that contains it, and the blocks are then assigned to folds as grid cells are. block_size, block_nx/block_ny, block_multiplier and boundary have nothing to act on and are ignored (logged); auto_range only compares the estimated range with the blocks. See the section "Supplied blocks". Blocks that mix dimensions or carry M are read in x and y, and params$blocks holds them in XY. An error for any other method.

balance_tol

A number of at least 1, default 3. For "block_kfold": the ratio of the largest fold's point count to the smallest's above which the folds are reported as imbalanced, with a warning (an R condition, also logged) that names both counts; Inf turns the check off. It is the tolerance of a check, not a target the packing aims for (see the section "Fold balance"), and params$balance_ratio carries the ratio achieved. For "knndm" it is a limit: a candidate whose largest fold holds more than balance_tol times the points of its smallest is set aside, so the folds returned are within it.

max_test

For "buffered_loo" and "nndm": optional whole number of at least 2. Folds are built for a random subset of that many held-out points (drawn under seed), and every row stays available for training, so each fold returned is the fold the full design has for that point. The model is then refitted max_test times and not n times, and the folds hold 4 * n * max_test bytes of row indices in place of 4 * n^2, which lets "buffered_loo" run on layers its storage limit otherwise refuses. It does not lift the 5,000-row limit of "nndm", whose cost is the matching itself; for that there is "knndm". For "nndm" the matching still runs over all n points and params describes all of them. area_of_applicability() needs every training row in a test fold and refuses a subset. Default NULL: every point is held out once. An error for the k-fold methods, whose number of folds is k.

Value

A list with:

method

The method used.

k

The number of folds built, which can differ from the k asked for (see k); length(folds) always equals it.

folds

A list with one element per fold, each a list of train and test row IDs: the values of the ..row_id column when the input has one, otherwise row positions.

assignment

A tibble with one row per observation kept: row_id (the same IDs) and fold, and for "block_kfold" a third column, block_id, the row of params$blocks the point fell in. With max_test, fold is NA for the rows not held out.

params

The settings and diagnostics of the build, below.

Every method's params carries seed, k_requested (the k asked for, NA when none was given) and row_probe, a small sample of row IDs and coordinates that every cv_*() function compares with the data it is handed, so folds built from a different layer of the same size are refused rather than applied. The methods that work in projected space add crs, the CRS the folds were built in (an "EPSG:code" string where there is one, otherwise the CRS's input definition). Every length in params (block_size, sac_range, buffer, median_buffer) is in that CRS's units, which for lon/lat input is a CRS ensure_projected() chose, not one you passed.

For "block_kfold" the block design comes with the folds:

  • blocks: an sf layer of the block polygons in the CRS the folds were built in. Its rows are not the rows of the layer the blocks came from: drop_empty_blocks = TRUE (the default) removes the blocks that hold no point and renumbers the rest, so with supplied blocks a nine-polygon layer of which three are empty comes back as six rows numbered 1 to 6. blocks$source_row is the row each one came from (a grid cell's index in the full grid_nx by grid_ny grid, or the row of the blocks argument), so blocks[params$blocks$source_row, ] recovers them with their own columns and in their own order. It runs from 1 to n_blocks and is the identity when nothing was dropped.

  • n_blocks and blocks_used: for a grid, n_blocks is grid_nx * grid_ny, the cells a boundary clips away included, and blocks_used the number of blocks returned.

  • block_sizes: the number of points in each block, indexed by block_id (zeros are empty blocks that drop_empty_blocks = FALSE kept); fold_blocks: a list with one integer vector per fold naming the blocks packed into it. Between them the folds account for every block once, empty ones included, so a fold's territory on the map is all of its blocks, and table(assignment$fold) can be traced back to the blocks it is made of. plot_folds() draws the blocks over the data.

  • block_width and block_height: the width and height of the grid cells built, before any clipping to a boundary (NA for supplied blocks). They are what block_size turned into: at least that size on an axis long enough to hold it, and the whole extent on an axis that is not.

  • blocks_supplied and boundary_supplied: whether the blocks came from blocks, and whether a boundary was given.

  • block_scale, balance_ratio, balance_tol, block_size, block_multiplier, sac_range and auto_range: the length compared with the range (see the section "Supplied blocks"), the balance achieved and allowed, and the sizing settings.

For "nndm", params carries the diagnostics named in the section "NNDM". For "knndm" it carries chosen ("random" or "clusters"), n_clusters (the number of clusters packed into the folds; NA for the random partition), clustering ("ward" or "kmeans+ward"; NA when no cluster count was tried), candidates (a data frame with one row per candidate, the random partition first: candidate, n_clusters, largest_fold, balance_ratio, admissible and W, which is NA for a candidate set aside), wasserstein, wasserstein_random and wasserstein_loo (the Wasserstein distance to the target of the folds returned, of the random partition among the candidates and of plain leave-one-out, in distance units), fold_sizes, balance_ratio, target_distances and realised_distances (one per prediction point, and one per row: its distance to the nearest point of another fold) with their medians and means, and the diagnostics "nndm" reports under the same names: max_ecdf_excess, max_ecdf_deficit, loo_ecdf_deficit, ecdf_deficit_tol, target_separated and target_out_of_reach, with short_of_target for the opposite case (see the section "kNNDM"). With max_test, params$max_test records the value.

Rows without a location (an empty point, or a coordinate that is not finite or lies beyond 1e150) are dropped before folding, with a logged warning naming the count; they appear in no fold and in no assignment row. The bound is read on the coordinates as given, and again after the projection for the methods that measure distance.

Fold methods

MethodHeld out in each foldNeedsSuits a map that
"random_kfold"a random 1/k of the rowskpredicts among the samples, over an area they cover evenly
"block_kfold"whole blocks of a grid, or of blocksk; block_size or auto_range to size the gridpredicts into unsampled gaps about as wide as the blocks
"buffered_loo"one point, with its neighbours within buffer left out of trainingbufferpredicts at a known distance from the data
"leave_location_out"every row of one or more locationsgroup_varpredicts at sites with no measurements, from repeated measurements at others
"nndm"one point, with neighbours left out to match the prediction distancesprediction_points; at most 5,000 rowspredicts at known locations, with a model cheap enough to refit once per point
"knndm"k folds matched to the prediction distancesprediction_pointspredicts at known locations, from a large layer or with a costly model

A cross-validated error is the error at the distances the folds put between the held-out points and their training data. It reads low for predictions made farther from the data than the held-out points sit, and high for predictions made closer, so which folds to use depends on where the model will predict. fold_separation() with prediction_points compares the two distances, and method = "nndm" and "knndm" build folds matched to them.

"random_kfold" ignores geography: a held-out point keeps most of its neighbours in the training data, so the score is the error of predicting among the samples. That is the error of a map over an area the samples cover evenly, and it reads low for predictions made farther from the data, such as a map of a whole region from clustered samples. "block_kfold" holds out whole blocks, so the held-out points sit farther from their training data the wider the blocks are, and the score is the error of predicting into unsampled gaps of that size; for a map of an area the samples cover, it reads high. "buffered_loo" holds out one point at a time and excludes everything within a fixed buffer from its training set. "leave_location_out" groups by group_var, so all observations from a location share a fold.

Block size and the autocorrelation range

With block_size, each axis of the extent gets as many blocks as leave every block at least that long, so on an axis at least as long as block_size the blocks are from one to just under two times this size. An axis shorter than block_size is spanned by one row or column of blocks as long as the extent there: a 39.8 km by 5 km extent with block_size = 10000 gets three blocks 13.3 km wide and 5 km tall. A size that leaves fewer than k blocks holding points returns that many folds, with a warning (see k); one that leaves a single block is an error. Both name the largest size that still gives k folds. A size in the wrong unit asks for an enormous grid, so a request above 1,000,000 blocks is refused with an error naming the grid dimensions, the extent and the CRS's units.

Without block_size or auto_range, the grid is sized from the extent and block_multiplier (or block_nx and block_ny) alone, with no regard to the autocorrelation range of the data. The wider the blocks, the farther the held-out points sit from their training data. When blocks are smaller than the autocorrelation range, each held-out point still has training data within the range. The score is then the error of predicting that close to the data. It reads low for a map whose locations lie farther from the samples, and is the error of a map whose locations lie as close.

block_size sets a minimum block edge length in CRS units, and auto_range = TRUE estimates the range with estimate_sac_range() and uses it as that minimum. When a response is given and the blocks are smaller than the estimated range, make_folds() warns and gives the block size of the range. When blocks of that size leave fewer than k folds on this layout, the warning also names the largest size that still gives k folds and a method that needs no block size ("nndm", or "knndm" above 5,000 rows).

Sizing blocks from the autocorrelation range is the recommendation of Roberts et al. (2017) and what blockCV (Valavi et al. 2019) automates. blockCV takes the fitted variogram's range parameter as the block size; auto_range takes the effective range that estimate_sac_range() returns, three times that parameter for an exponential fit, so its blocks are larger than blockCV's from the same variogram. The estimate is the omnidirectional range. On a field known to be anisotropic, pass block_size = max(attr(r, "directional_fitted"), na.rm = TRUE) yourself after checking attr(r, "directional_status") (see the section "Directional ranges and anisotropy" in estimate_sac_range()).

Range-sized blocks do not fit every layout. On a square extent at k = 5, a range up to a third of the side gives five folds; up to half, a 2 by 2 grid and four folds, returned with the "spatialkit_k_reduced" warning. Above half the extent in both directions there is room for a single block, and make_folds() stops with an error naming the size rather than return one fold with an empty training set. The warning and the error name the largest block size that still gives k folds on this layout and how far below the range it is. When no range is identified, the geometric grid is used instead, with a warning that gives the reason. When the range is used, a message states the grid and the block size built.

NNDM

"nndm" implements the distance-matching principle of Milà et al. (2022): it sizes the exclusion around each held-out point, with no fixed buffer, so that the distribution of distances from the held-out points to their training data approaches the distribution of distances from the prediction locations to the training data.

The procedure is the paper's, and it is deterministic. Let \(G_{ij}\) be the empirical distribution of prediction-to-nearest-training distances and \(G_j^*\) the distribution of each held-out point's distance to its nearest remaining training point. Starting from plain leave-one-out, the point with the smallest \(G_j^*\) at which the realised distribution exceeds the target (\(G_j^*(r) > G_{ij}(r)\)) has its nearest training neighbour removed, and this repeats until no such point remains, within two limits. A point is matched only while its nearest-neighbour distance is at most phi (default: the largest prediction distance, since a training point already farther than every prediction distance has nothing to match), so the exclusion that takes it past phi is its last and a realised distance can exceed phi by up to one neighbour step. And no fold's training set is stripped below min_train of the data.

It differs from CAST::nndm() in two details, so the folds agree closely with CAST's but not exactly. The removal rule is strict: a neighbour is removed whenever the realised distribution exceeds the target, where CAST removes one only while the realised distribution, less the point about to move, is still at or above the target. The rule here therefore removes up to one point more per distance value, erring towards held-out distances longer than the target. And ties in \(G_j^*\) are broken by the points' coordinates, not by their row index as in CAST, so the folds do not depend on the order of the rows (see the section "Numerical tolerances").

Where neither limit binds, the realised distribution of nearest-neighbour distances is never shorter than the target: \(G_j^*(r) \le G_{ij}(r)\) up to the granularity of the neighbour distances, which is the property the method exists to deliver. It is a statement about the distance to the one nearest training point. A learner that draws on several neighbours (a forest, a k-nearest-neighbour mean, a kriging neighbourhood) also depends on how far the second and later neighbours are, which NNDM does not match, so on clustered samples its cross-validated error can still read low for the prediction points with the nearest-neighbour distances matched exactly. Beyond phi no matching is attempted. min_train is different: when the prediction locations lie farther from the samples than a fold can be made to hold out (clustered samples and a prediction domain well beyond them, the layout NNDM is meant for), it stops the matching early and the realised distances stay too short. params$n_at_min_train counts the folds held at the floor while still closer than the target allows, and make_folds() warns when that leaves more than one point's worth of excess at or below phi. Lower min_train to match further, or read the cross-validated score as an upper bound on performance at the prediction locations. params$max_ecdf_excess reports the largest remaining excess; compare params$target_median with params$realised_median as well.

The match has a second side. params$max_ecdf_deficit is the largest amount by which the target distribution runs above the realised one, the mirror of params$max_ecdf_excess: the share of prediction points within some distance of the data that the folds do not reproduce. Part of it is the granularity of the matching. Excluding a neighbour moves a held-out point out to its next remaining neighbour, and on clustered samples that can be the next cluster, well past the prediction distances.

The other part no setting reaches. Excluding neighbours can only lengthen a held-out distance, so when the prediction points sit nearer to the data than the samples sit to each other (prediction points among the samples, or a regular sample predicted between its nodes) the folds returned are plain leave-one-out and are still farther from their training data than the prediction points are. The cross-validated error is then pessimistic for those prediction points: an upper bound on the error there. params$loo_ecdf_deficit is the largest amount by which the target distribution runs above that of plain leave-one-out. When it exceeds params$ecdf_deficit_tol, three times \(\sqrt{1/n + 1/m}\) for \(n\) folds and \(m\) prediction points (about three times the chance difference between two samples of one distribution), make_folds() raises a warning of class "spatialkit_nndm_out_of_reach" and sets params$target_out_of_reach to TRUE.

On small samples no deficit can exceed that tolerance. A deficit is a difference of two shares, so it is at most 1, and the tolerance is 1 or more whenever \(nm/(n+m) \le 9\): for nine folds or fewer whatever the number of prediction points, and for up to eighteen folds with as many prediction points. There the same warning is raised in one case only, complete separation: every prediction point nearer to the data than any sample is to its nearest other sample, by more than one part in ten million (a deficit of 1), provided the two sets are large enough for that ordering to mean something, taken as choose(n + m, n) >= 1000 ways of interleaving them (17 prediction points for 3 folds, 7 for 6 folds, 4 for 12 folds). params$target_separated records the ordering whether or not it was enough to warn, and the warning's condition carries it as separated. With very few samples it can hold for a grid over the samples' own extent, because a few points hug the box they span; the folds are then farther than the grid all the same. A partial shortfall on such a sample (most prediction points nearer than leave-one-out reaches, not all) is not warned about, since no difference of shares exceeds a tolerance of 1 or more. Compare params$target_median with params$realised_median.

params$wasserstein is the Wasserstein distance between the target and realised distributions, in distance units, and params$wasserstein_loo the same for plain leave-one-out: equal when nothing was excluded, smaller when the matching helped.

kNNDM

"knndm" is the k-fold version of NNDM (Linnenbrink et al. 2024): k folds, and so k model fits, whose held-out distances are as close to the same target as a set of candidates allows. It has no row limit, and is the method to use above the 5,000 rows "nndm" takes or when a model is too costly to refit once per point. Below that it matches less closely than NNDM, since a fold design has far fewer degrees of freedom than one exclusion set per point.

The candidates are a random k-fold partition (the one "random_kfold" builds with the same seed) and, for each of up to 50 cluster counts spaced evenly on the log scale from k to one fewer than the number of distinct locations, the samples clustered on their coordinates and the clusters merged into k folds. Few large clusters give folds that are whole areas, far from their training data; many small ones approach the random partition. Up to 4,000 points the clustering is Ward's (stats::hclust(method = "ward.D2")), cut at each count. Above that, where the n by n distance matrix it needs is too large, k-means first reduces the samples to 4,000 groups (Lloyd's algorithm from random sample locations, at most ten passes) and Ward's method is continued from those groups; a count above 4,000 is a k-means run of its own. params$clustering says which ("ward" or "kmeans+ward"). Clusters are merged by the packing "block_kfold" uses for its blocks, largest first and each to the fold with the fewest points so far (see the section "Fold balance"). CAST::knndm() merges clusters by a rule of its own, which this was not checked against, so the folds are not expected to equal CAST's.

Each candidate is scored by the Wasserstein distance \(W\) between its held-out distances (each point's distance to the nearest point of another fold) and the target distances, in the unit of the layer, and the smallest \(W\) is returned; of the candidates within one part in ten million of the smallest, the earliest in params$candidates. A candidate is set aside without being scored when its largest fold leaves less than min_train of the rows for training or holds more than balance_tol times the points of its smallest; the random partition is always kept. So params$wasserstein is never above params$wasserstein_random, the \(W\) of that random partition, and params$candidates lists every candidate with its cluster count, fold sizes and \(W\). params$chosen is "random" when no clustering came closer, as for samples spread evenly over the prediction area. Read \(W\) against the mean target distance; it has no sign, so it measures the mismatch in either direction. With few folds a random partition can itself be farther than the target, since each fold trains on 1 - 1/k of the points. Construction time grows with the number of points and of folds.

Two cases are warned about, each with a condition class. When the prediction points sit nearer to the data than a sample is to its nearest other sample, no fold design reaches them, since a held-out point is never nearer to its training data than that; the test is the one "nndm" applies, the warning has the same class, "spatialkit_nndm_out_of_reach", and what comes back is the random partition or a candidate as fine as one. In the other direction, the closest candidate can still be short of the target: prediction points well beyond the samples lie farther from the data than k folds of those samples can be held apart. When the mean held-out distance of the folds returned is below the mean target distance by more than a quarter of it and by at least half of \(W\) (the test fold_separation() words as "closer"), make_folds() raises a warning of class "spatialkit_knndm_short_of_target" and sets params$short_of_target: the cross-validated error then tends to read low for the prediction points. Fewer folds hold out larger areas. Short of either warning the folds can still differ from the target at some distances; params$max_ecdf_excess and params$max_ecdf_deficit give the largest difference each way, and fold_separation() reads the folds against the same prediction points fold by fold.

Supplied blocks

A polygon layer passed as blocks is aligned to the points the way boundary is, and then brought into the CRS the folds are built in (see spatialkit-geometry). A point inside more than one block is given the first (lowest row) that contains it, as for a point on the shared edge of two grid cells, and a point within the margin of a block's edge (see the section "Numerical tolerances") counts as inside it. When the blocks that caught such a point share area instead of an edge, the layer overlaps and is not a partition, and make_folds() warns. A point inside no block is assigned to the nearest one, by distance to the polygon itself; a point the same distance from two blocks, to one part in ten million or that margin, goes to the lower row. The count of such points is warned about, unless they sit within a millionth of the extent of a block, an edge that reprojection or clipping moved by a rounding error. Blocks that hold no point are dropped when drop_empty_blocks = TRUE, and k is lowered to the number of blocks that hold points when that is smaller.

params$n_blocks is the number of blocks before empties were dropped and params$blocks_used the number after (so with drop_empty_blocks = FALSE the two are equal, and sum(params$block_sizes > 0) is how many hold points); params$grid_nx and params$grid_ny are NA. params$block_scale is the median, over the blocks that hold points, of the side of the square with the block's area. A polygon has no single edge length, so that is the length compared with the autocorrelation range for the warning on blocks smaller than the range.

Every set of cells build_tessellation() builds can be a block design here, including Voronoi cells around get_voronoi_seeds(method = "kmeans") seeds, which adapt to the density of the points.

Fold balance

"block_kfold" and "knndm" balance the number of points per fold by packing: blocks (for "knndm", clusters of the samples) are taken largest first and each goes to the fold with the fewest points so far, ties broken at random. This is the longest-processing-time rule for multiway partitioning, and make_folds() offers no search over other packings. The remedy for an imbalance past balance_tol is the block design: smaller blocks, or blocks that adapt to the density of the points, passed through blocks. Density-adaptive blocks are smaller where points are dense, so check params$block_scale against the autocorrelation range as you would a grid.

"knndm" chooses its clusters, so for it balance_tol is a limit: a clustering whose packing exceeds it is not a candidate, and the folds returned are within it (params$fold_sizes, params$balance_ratio).

The other methods do not balance point counts. "random_kfold" is balanced by construction (fold sizes differ by at most one); "buffered_loo" and "nndm" hold out one point per fold; "leave_location_out" gives each fold the same number of locations (to within one), so folds differ by as much as the locations' sizes do.

Numerical tolerances

A point on the edge two grid cells share goes to the lower one, the cell with the lower index in the full grid (params$blocks$source_row; the grid is numbered along each row from the bottom left, so the cell to the left or below). A point is on an edge while it lies within one part in 1e10 of the largest coordinate of the points and the blocks from it (0.44 mm at a UTM northing of 4,400 km), at most a millionth of the diagonal of their bounding box and at least four times the spacing of doubles at that coordinate, so points on the grid lines of a lattice are blocked alike in any unit or origin. A point in no cell of a clipped grid goes to the cell with the nearest centroid, and to the lower of two whose centroids are as near to one part in ten million or that margin. The same margin decides whether a point lies on a boundary or inside a supplied block.

A block shorter than block_size by no more than one part in ten million counts as that long, so a size of exactly the axis over a whole number gives that number of blocks in any unit. A neighbour of a "buffered_loo" point at the buffer distance is excluded, and so is one over it by rounding: a squared distance within one part in ten million of the buffer's square (a distance about one part in twenty million over the buffer) counts as at it, so a lattice whose spacing divides the buffer gives the same folds in any unit or origin.

NNDM counts distances within one part in ten million of each other as equal, when the held-out distances are counted, compared with the target and phi, and put in order. Equal ones are taken by the column of the point (first coordinates within that part of the extent of the points count as one), then its second coordinate, counted the same way, then its row. Each point's neighbours are put in order by the same rule, so of neighbours that are equally far away the same one is excluded first. The folds are then the same in another unit or with another origin as long as no coordinate moves by more than about a two-hundred-millionth of the distance between neighbouring locations.

The clusterings of kNNDM read the coordinates centred on the middle of their bounding box, divided by its diagonal and rounded to 2^-30 of it (about a billionth), as the "kmeans" partition hands them to stats::kmeans(); on a lattice many merges and many assignments tie exactly, and the last bits of the coordinates, which move with the unit and the origin, would settle them. A point as near two k-means centres to one part in ten million goes to the lower-numbered one: a squared distance ties with the least when it is no more than the square of the least distance lengthened by a margin, plus one part in ten million of the least squared distance, the margin one part in 1e10 of the largest coordinate of the centres in that frame, at most a millionth of the diagonal of their bounding box and at least four times the spacing of doubles at that coordinate. The clusters are then the same in another unit or with another origin, but for a location within its own rounding noise of the middle of a step.

Points so far from the origin of their coordinates that doubles there are spaced more than a millionth of the points' extent apart are held to that spacing, and so are the edges of the blocks laid over them (see the section "Coordinates far from the origin" in spatialkit-geometry). With method = "block_kfold" or "buffered_loo" the folds are made, and a warning of class "spatialkit_xy_imprecise" gives the spacing and the extent.

References

Linnenbrink, J., Mila, C., Ludwig, M. and Meyer, H. (2024). kNNDM CV: k-fold nearest-neighbour distance matching cross-validation for map accuracy estimation. Geoscientific Model Development 17, 5897-5912. doi:10.5194/gmd-17-5897-2024

Mila, C., Mateu, J., Pebesma, E. and Meyer, H. (2022). Nearest neighbour distance matching Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation for map validation. Methods in Ecology and Evolution 13, 1304-1316. doi:10.1111/2041-210X.13851

Roberts, D. R., Bahn, V., Ciuti, S., Boyce, M. S., Elith, J., Guillera-Arroita, G., Hauenstein, S., Lahoz-Monfort, J. J., Schroder, B., Thuiller, W., Warton, D. I., Wintle, B. A., Hartig, F. and Dormann, C. F. (2017). Cross-validation strategies for data with temporal, spatial, hierarchical, or phylogenetic structure. Ecography 40, 913-929. doi:10.1111/ecog.02881

Valavi, R., Elith, J., Lahoz-Monfort, J. J. and Guillera-Arroita, G. (2019). blockCV: An R package for generating spatially or environmentally separated folds for k-fold cross-validation of species distribution models. Methods in Ecology and Evolution 10, 225-232. doi:10.1111/2041-210X.13107

See also

plot_folds() to map the folds, fold_separation() to measure how far the held-out points sit from their training data, cv_spatial() to score a model on them, and cv_block_size_sweep() to cross-validate at a ladder of block sizes.

Other folds: cv_block_size_sweep(), fold_separation(), plot_folds()

Examples

library(sf)
set.seed(1)
pts <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(30, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(30, 0, 1000)),
  coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632
)
folds <- make_folds(pts, k = 3, method = "block_kfold", seed = 42)
folds$assignment          # fold and block of each row
#> # A tibble: 30 × 3
#>    row_id  fold block_id
#>     <int> <int>    <int>
#>  1      1     1        4
#>  2      2     3        8
#>  3      3     1        5
#>  4      4     2        3
#>  5      5     3        7
#>  6      6     2        9
#>  7      7     2        9
#>  8      8     3        2
#>  9      9     3        8
#> 10     10     1        4
#> # ℹ 20 more rows
lengths(folds$folds[[1]]) # the train and test row IDs of fold 1
#> train  test 
#>    20    10 
folds$params$block_sizes  # points per block
#> [1] 2 2 2 3 5 3 4 4 5
folds$params$fold_blocks  # the blocks each fold holds
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 5 4 1
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 9 6 3
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> [1] 7 8 2
#> 

# Buffered leave-one-out: neighbours within 100 m left out of training.
loo <- make_folds(pts, method = "buffered_loo", buffer = 100)
loo$k                     # one fold per point
#> [1] 30

# Three folds matched to the distances from a prediction grid to
# clustered samples.
set.seed(2)
cx <- runif(6, 0, 1e4); cy <- runif(6, 0, 1e4)
xy <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:6, function(i)
  cbind(cx[i] + rnorm(15, 0, 200), cy[i] + rnorm(15, 0, 200))))
cl <- st_as_sf(data.frame(x = 5e5 + xy[, 1], y = 5e6 + xy[, 2]),
               coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)
grid <- st_make_grid(cl, n = c(20, 20), what = "centers")
km <- make_folds(cl, k = 3, method = "knndm", prediction_points = grid,
                 seed = 42)
km$params[c("chosen", "n_clusters", "wasserstein", "wasserstein_random")]
#> $chosen
#> [1] "clusters"
#> 
#> $n_clusters
#> [1] 18
#> 
#> $wasserstein
#> [1] 741.4627
#> 
#> $wasserstein_random
#> [1] 1108.152
#>
